title: Food, Markets and Cooking
overview: Buying food is the thing you will do most often in a language that is not yours, and it has its own small grammar. This unit teaches how to ask for an amount of something, when to use some and when to use any, how to read a set of instructions that gives orders rather than statements, and how to put steps in an order somebody can follow. It ends with a food label, because a label carries two dates that mean different things and one of them matters much more than the other.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. It covers all four patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 1 builds on the countable and uncountable idea from Unit 4 — it does not teach it again.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a food label.
Do the Practice. Practice 5 needs a real label from your kitchen.
Record yourself ordering five things at a market.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
Buying food is probably the thing you will do most often in English, and it has a small grammar of its own.
Four patterns.
The first is how to ask for an amount. In Unit 4 you learned that some things can be counted and some cannot — four oranges, but not four rices. This unit is what you do about it when you want to buy the ones you cannot count.
English puts a container or a measure in front. A packet of rice. A bottle of milk. A kilo of meat. A slice of bread. A tin of fish. A piece of cheese.
The shape is always the same: a, then the container, then of, then the thing. And the little word of is the one that disappears — a packet rice is the mistake, and it is the only mistake this pattern has.
Once you use a container, the container is countable even if the thing inside is not. Two bottles of milk. Three packets of rice. So you can count anything, as long as you count the containers.
Second pattern: some and any. These say an amount without a number, and English chooses between them by the kind of sentence, not by the amount.
Some in a positive statement. I have some rice. There is some milk.
Any in a negative and in most questions. I do not have any rice. Is there any milk?
And one exception you will use constantly: when you are offering something or asking for something, English uses some even though it is a question. Would you like some tea? Can I have some bread? That is because you are not really asking whether it exists — you are offering or requesting.
So: positive, some. Negative, any. Question, usually any — but some when you are offering or asking for it.
Third pattern: instructions. A recipe does not say you put the rice in the pan. It says put the rice in the pan.
This is the imperative, and you met it in Unit 3 for exercise instructions. Here it is the same shape doing a different job. The verb comes first, with nobody in front of it. Cut. Add. Boil. Mix. Heat.
For the negative, put do not in front. Do not add salt. Do not boil it for more than ten minutes.
You will read this shape far more often than you say it — on packets, on machines, on medicine, on official notices. Learning to read it quickly is worth more than learning to produce it.
Fourth pattern: order. First, then, after that, next, finally.
A set of steps without these words is a list. With them it is a sequence, and a sequence can be followed by somebody who was not watching you.
First, boil the water. Then add the rice. After that, cook it for ten minutes. Finally, take it off the heat.
Notice each one is followed by a comma when it starts the sentence. That comma is small and it makes the instruction much easier to read.
One last thing, and it is about labels rather than grammar. A food label carries two kinds of date, and they do not mean the same thing. Use by is about safety. Best before is about quality. Food after its best before date is usually fine; food after its use by date may not be. That single difference is the most useful thing on the label, and the last text in this unit is about finding it.
Go to Patterns.

words.meaning: Small white or brown grains that are boiled and eaten.
words.example: I need a packet of rice.
practice: There is some rice in the cupboard.
We do not have any rice.
Boil the rice for ten minutes.
Rice is cheaper at the market.
words.tutor: Ask for rice in two ways: with a container and without one. Notice which sounds more natural in a shop.

words.meaning: A food made from flour and baked, usually in a loaf.
words.example: Can I have some bread, please?
practice: There is no bread left.
I buy bread every morning.
Cut two slices of bread.
The bread is fresher at the market.
words.tutor: Ask for bread as a request, then ask whether there is any. Notice which takes some and which takes any.

words.meaning: The white liquid from cows and other animals, drunk and used in cooking.
words.example: We need a bottle of milk.
practice: Is there any milk?
I do not take milk in my tea.
Add a little milk.
The milk is past its use by date.
words.tutor: Ask whether there is milk, and answer both yes and no. Check which word each answer needs.

words.meaning: The flesh of an animal, eaten as food.
words.example: How much is the meat per kilo?
practice: I do not eat much meat.
Cook the meat for an hour.
The meat is fresh today.
There is some meat in the fridge.
words.tutor: Ask the price of meat per kilo. Use the price question from Unit 4.

words.meaning: An animal that lives in water, eaten as food.
words.example: A tin of fish is cheap and quick.
practice: Is there any fish left?
The fish is very fresh.
I cook fish twice a week.
Do not cook the fish for too long.
words.tutor: Say how often you eat fish. Use a frequency word from Unit 5.

words.meaning: Plants or parts of plants eaten as food, such as onions and carrots.
words.example: I buy vegetables at the market.
practice: Cut the vegetables into small pieces.
There are no vegetables in the fridge.
Vegetables are cheaper here.
Add the vegetables after the meat.
words.tutor: Say where you buy vegetables and why there. Use because.

words.meaning: A place, often outdoors, where many people sell food and other goods.
words.example: The market is open on Saturdays.
practice: I go to the market every week.
The market is cheaper than the shop.
There is a market in the next street.
The market closes at two.
words.tutor: Say when the market is open near you, and how often you go.

words.meaning: A small open shop at a market, usually a table with goods on it.
words.example: The fish stall is at the end.
practice: That stall is always busy.
She has a stall at the market.
Which stall sells vegetables?
The stall opens at six in the morning.
words.starter: The fish stall is at the
words.tutor: Ask which stall sells something. Use the question form from Unit 3.

words.meaning: The paper or printing on a product that says what it is and what is in it.
words.example: Read the label before you buy it.
practice: The label says use by Friday.
There is no label on this one.
The price is on the label.
Check the label for the weight.
words.tutor: Say two things you would check on a label before buying something.

words.meaning: Recently made, picked or caught; not old and not frozen.
words.example: The bread is fresh today.
practice: Is the fish fresh?
Fresh vegetables are better.
It is not fresh — look at the date.
The market has the freshest fruit.
words.tutor: Ask whether something is fresh, and say how you would know.

words.meaning: To ask for something you want to buy.
words.example: I would like to order two kilos.
practice: She ordered the same as me.
Can I order it for Friday?
I ordered too much.
Order it before Thursday.
words.tutor: Order three things with amounts. Use a container for at least one.

words.meaning: A line of people waiting their turn.
words.example: There is a long queue at that stall.
practice: I waited in the queue for ten minutes.
The queue is shorter now.
Join the queue at the back.
There is never a queue on Tuesdays.
words.starter: There is a long queue at
words.tutor: Ask whether you are in the right queue. Note the spelling — four letters after the q are silent.

words.meaning: A small paper or plastic container with something inside.
words.example: A packet of rice, please.
practice: There are two packets in the cupboard.
The packet says boil for ten minutes.
This packet is nearly empty.
How much is a packet of tea?
words.tutor: Ask for three different things by the packet. Check you said of every time.

words.meaning: A tall container for liquid, usually glass or plastic.
words.example: Two bottles of milk, please.
practice: The bottle is empty.
A bottle of water costs very little.
Put the bottles in the bag.
There is one bottle left.
words.tutor: Say a bottle of and two bottles of. Notice the container takes the plural, not the liquid.

words.meaning: A sealed metal container for food that keeps for a long time.
words.example: A tin of fish is useful to have.
practice: There are three tins in the cupboard.
Open the tin carefully.
A tin lasts for years.
How much is a tin of tomatoes?
words.tutor: Say what you keep in tins and why. Use because.

words.meaning: A thin flat piece cut from something larger.
words.example: Two slices of bread, please.
practice: Cut a slice for me.
One slice is enough.
The slices are too thick.
A slice of bread and some tea.
words.tutor: Ask for a number of slices of something. Notice it is slices OF, not slices bread.

words.meaning: A part of something, cut or broken off.
words.example: A piece of fish, please.
practice: Cut it into six pieces.
This piece is too big.
There is one piece left.
A piece of paper and a pen.
words.tutor: Piece works with almost anything. Say four things you could ask for by the piece.

words.meaning: A number of things growing or fastened together, such as bananas or keys.
words.example: A bunch of bananas, please.
practice: That bunch is too small.
I bought two bunches.
A bunch of keys was on the table.
How much is a bunch?
words.tutor: Say two things that come in bunches. Ask the price of one.

words.meaning: To prepare food using heat.
words.example: Cook it for twenty minutes.
practice: I cook every evening.
She cooks better than I do.
Do not cook the fish too long.
Who cooks in your house?
words.tutor: Say how long to cook something. Then say who cooks in your home.

words.meaning: To heat a liquid until it bubbles, or to cook food in bubbling water.
words.example: First, boil the water.
practice: Boil the rice for ten minutes.
The water is boiling.
Do not let it boil over.
Boil it, then add the vegetables.
words.tutor: Give two boiling instructions, using first and then.

words.meaning: To divide something with a knife.
words.example: Cut the vegetables into small pieces.
practice: Cut it in half.
Be careful when you cut it.
I cut my finger.
Cut two slices of bread.
words.tutor: Give three cutting instructions with different amounts.

words.meaning: To put something in with something else.
words.example: Then add the rice.
practice: Add a little salt.
Do not add too much water.
After that, add the vegetables.
Add the meat last.
words.tutor: Give four add instructions in order, using first, then, after that and finally.

words.meaning: To put things together so they combine.
words.example: Mix it well.
practice: Mix the vegetables and the rice.
Do not mix them yet.
Mix everything in a large pan.
Mix it and leave it for five minutes.
words.tutor: Say two mixing instructions, one positive and one negative.

words.meaning: To make something hot.
words.example: Heat the oil first.
practice: Heat it for two minutes.
Do not heat it again.
Heat the pan before you add anything.
Take it off the heat.
words.tutor: Notice heat is both a verb and a noun here. Use it both ways.

words.meaning: A round metal container used for cooking on a stove.
words.example: Put it in a large pan.
practice: The pan is too small.
Heat the pan first.
Wash the pan afterwards.
There is one pan in the kitchen.
words.tutor: Say what size pan you need and why.

words.meaning: A tool with a blade, used for cutting. More than one: knives.
words.example: Use a sharp knife.
practice: The knife is not sharp enough.
Put the knives in the drawer.
Be careful with the knife.
I need a bigger knife.
words.tutor: Knife becomes knives in the plural, and the k is silent. Say both forms.

words.meaning: A flat dish that food is served on.
words.example: There are four plates in the cupboard.
practice: Put it on a plate.
The plate is hot.
Wash the plates after dinner.
One plate is broken.
words.starter: There are four plates in the
words.tutor: Say how many plates there are somewhere, using there are.

words.meaning: A tool with a small bowl on a handle, used for eating and stirring.
words.example: Mix it with a spoon.
practice: Add two spoons of sugar.
The spoon is in the drawer.
Use a large spoon.
There are no clean spoons.
words.tutor: Notice a spoon of something is also an amount. Use it both ways.

words.meaning: The closed box in a cooker where food is baked.
words.example: Put it in the oven for an hour.
practice: The oven is not working.
Heat the oven first.
Take it out of the oven.
There is no oven in this kitchen.
words.starter: Put it in the oven for
words.tutor: Give an oven instruction with a time. Use for.

readings.title: Buying Food in a Language That Is Not Yours
readings.passage:
Buying food is the thing you will do most often in English, and it is also the easiest thing to do badly for years without noticing.
Here is why. You can buy food with almost no language at all. You point, you hold up two fingers, you hand over a note and you take the change. It works. Nobody minds. And you learn nothing, because you never said anything.
So make it harder on purpose.
Say the amount out loud, even when pointing would be quicker. Two kilos, please. A packet of rice. Three slices.
Ask one question you did not need to ask. Is this fresh? How much per kilo? Have you got any smaller ones?
Repeat the price back before you pay. This one you should do anyway.
A market is a good place to practise for three reasons. The conversations are short, so a mistake costs you nothing. They repeat, so you get the same sentence many times in one morning. And the person you are talking to wants the exchange to work, because they want to sell you something.
One warning. When you are new, everything sounds fast, and the number is the part that matters. If you did not catch it, ask. You learned how in Unit 3.

readings.title: How to Read a Recipe
readings.passage:
A recipe is written in a shape you will meet again and again — on packets, on machines, on medicine, on official forms.
It gives orders, not statements. It does not say you boil the water. It says boil the water. The verb comes first and nobody is named, because the instruction is for whoever is reading it.
A recipe has two parts, and reading them in the wrong order is the usual mistake.
The first part is what you need. Read all of it before you start. This sounds obvious and almost nobody does it, and that is how you get halfway through and discover there is no oil.
The second part is what you do, in order. Each step usually begins with a word that says where you are: first, then, after that, next, finally.
Here is one, written out.
First, heat the oil in a large pan.
Then cut the vegetables into small pieces.
After that, add the vegetables to the pan and mix them well.
Next, add a little water and boil it for ten minutes.
Finally, add salt and take it off the heat.
Notice two things. Every step is one instruction, not three. And every ordering word is followed by a comma.
One more thing worth knowing. Times on a packet are minimums, not promises. Boil for ten minutes usually means at least ten. Check it yourself before you trust it.

readings.title: Food Label
readings.setting: The label on the back of a packet of soup.
readings.passage:
VEGETABLE SOUP
Net weight: 400 g   (2 portions of 200 g)

INGREDIENTS
Water, carrot (18%), potato (14%), onion,
tomato, salt, sunflower oil, wheat flour,
black pepper.

CONTAINS: WHEAT
May contain traces of milk.

NUTRITION            per 100 g     per portion
Energy                  62 kcal       124 kcal
Fat                      1.8 g         3.6 g
Salt                     0.9 g         1.8 g

USE BY:        14 MAY
BEST BEFORE:   —

STORAGE
Keep refrigerated below 5 degrees.
Once opened, eat within 2 days.
Do not freeze.

PREPARATION
Empty into a pan. Heat gently, stirring.
Do not boil.
Heat until piping hot. Do not reheat.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say you can buy food for years without learning anything?
comprehension.a: Because you can point, hold up fingers and hand over money without saying anything.
comprehension.why: The text calls this out precisely because it works — the transaction succeeds and no language is used, so nothing is learned.

comprehension.q: What three things does the text tell you to do to make it harder on purpose?
comprehension.a: Say the amount out loud, ask one question you did not need to ask, and repeat the price back.
comprehension.why: All three are listed in order. The third one the text says you should be doing anyway, from Unit 4.

comprehension.q: The text gives three reasons a market is good for practising. What is the third?
comprehension.a: The person wants the exchange to work, because they want to sell you something.
comprehension.why: This is the least obvious of the three, and it is the reason a market is easier than a classroom conversation — the other person is motivated to understand you.

comprehension.q: How is an instruction different from a statement?
comprehension.a: The verb comes first and nobody is named — it says boil the water, not you boil the water.
comprehension.why: The text states the difference directly, and this shape appears on packets, machines and official notices, not only in recipes.

comprehension.q: Which part of a recipe does the text say to read before you start, and why?
comprehension.a: The list of what you need, so you do not get halfway through and find something missing.
comprehension.why: The text says almost nobody does this. It is the difference between a recipe working and stopping in the middle.

comprehension.q: The text says times on a packet are minimums, not promises. What should you do?
comprehension.a: Check it yourself before you trust it — boil for ten minutes usually means at least ten.
comprehension.why: This is an inference about how instructions are written rather than about language, and it is the kind of thing nobody says out loud.

comprehension.q: How much does the whole packet weigh, and how many portions is that?
comprehension.a: 400 grams, which is two portions of 200 grams.
comprehension.why: Both are on the second line. The portion size matters for the nutrition table further down.

comprehension.q: The label gives a use by date but no best before date. What does that tell you?
comprehension.a: That this is about safety, not quality — it should not be eaten after 14 May.
comprehension.why: Use by is a safety date and best before is a quality one. A product carrying only a use by date is one where the date matters for more than taste.

comprehension.q: The salt figure says 0.9 g per 100 g. How much salt is in one portion?
comprehension.a: 1.8 grams, because a portion is 200 grams — twice 100.
comprehension.why: The table gives both columns, but the per portion figure only makes sense once you know a portion is 200 g from the line at the top. Reading the per 100 g column alone halves the real amount.

comprehension.q: You open the packet on 10 May and use half. When must you eat the rest?
comprehension.a: By 12 May — within two days of opening, which comes before the use by date of 14 May.
comprehension.why: Two rules apply at once and the tighter one wins. The use by date is not the answer here, and that is exactly the trap.

grammar.title: A packet of, a bottle of, a slice of
grammar.explanation: In Unit 4 you learned that some things cannot be counted — you cannot say four rices. This is what English does about it: it puts a container or a measure in front, and then you count the containers.
grammar.rule:
a + container + of + thing

  a packet of rice      a bottle of milk
  a tin of fish         a slice of bread
  a piece of cheese     a bunch of bananas
  a kilo of meat        a spoon of sugar

The container is countable:
  two bottles of milk · three packets of rice
grammar.workedExample:
You want to buy rice. How do you ask?
1. Can rice be counted? No — two rices is not English.
2. So put a container in front. Rice comes in packets.
3. Build it: a … packet … of … rice.
4. Add the number if you want more than one — and the NUMBER goes on the container: two packets of rice.
Result: Two packets of rice, please.
Notice the s went on packets, not on rice. The container is the countable part.
grammar.mistake: The word of is the one that disappears — a packet rice instead of a packet of rice. It is the only real mistake this pattern has, and it is worth checking every time until it is automatic. The other slip is putting the plural on the wrong word: two packets of rice, never two packet of rices.
grammar.tip: Count the container, not the thing inside.
grammar.practice:
Complete each phrase.
1. a ____ of rice
2. a ____ of milk
3. two ____ of bread
4. a ____ of fish (metal container)
5. a ____ of bananas
6. three ____ of water
grammar.answers:
1. packet  2. bottle  3. slices  4. tin  5. bunch  6. bottles
Check two things. In 3 and 6 the s went on the container — slices and bottles — and not on bread or water. And every one of the six needs of after the container; if you left it out anywhere, that is the mistake to watch.

grammar.title: Some and any
grammar.explanation: Both say an amount without giving a number. English chooses between them by the kind of sentence, not by how much there is.
grammar.rule:
POSITIVE  → some
  I have some rice.
  There is some milk.

NEGATIVE  → any
  I do not have any rice.
  There is not any milk.

QUESTION  → any
  Is there any milk?
  Have you got any bread?

EXCEPTION — offering or asking for it → some
  Would you like some tea?
  Can I have some bread?
grammar.workedExample:
Which one: Can I have ____ bread, please?
1. Is it positive, negative or a question? A question.
2. Questions usually take any.
3. But wait — am I asking whether bread exists, or am I asking for bread? I am asking FOR it.
4. Requests and offers take some, even as questions.
Result: Can I have some bread, please?
Compare: Is there any bread? — that one really is asking whether it exists, so it takes any.
grammar.mistake: Using any in a request — can I have any bread sounds odd and slightly hopeless, as though you doubt there is any. The test is whether you are asking about existence or asking to be given something. Existence takes any; asking for it takes some.
grammar.tip: Offering or asking for it? Some. Otherwise, question means any.
grammar.practice:
Write some or any.
1. There is ____ rice in the cupboard.
2. We do not have ____ milk.
3. Is there ____ bread left?
4. Would you like ____ tea?
5. Can I have ____ water, please?
6. I did not buy ____ vegetables.
grammar.answers:
1. some  2. any  3. any  4. some  5. some  6. any
Numbers 4 and 5 are the exception at work — both are questions, but one is an offer and the other is a request, so both take some. Number 3 is a genuine question about whether bread exists, so it takes any.

grammar.title: Instructions: the verb comes first
grammar.explanation: You met this shape in Unit 3 for exercise instructions. Here it is the same form doing a different job: telling somebody how to do something. The verb comes first and nobody is named.
grammar.rule:
Boil the water.
Cut the vegetables.
Add a little salt.
Mix it well.
Heat the oil first.

Negative — do not in front:
  Do not boil it.
  Do not add too much water.
  Do not reheat.

No I, no you, nobody. Just the verb.
grammar.workedExample:
Turn this statement into an instruction: You put the rice in the pan.
1. Find the subject: You.
2. Remove it.
3. What is left starts with the verb: Put the rice in the pan.
Result: Put the rice in the pan.
For the negative, add do not at the front: Do not put the rice in the pan.
That is the whole operation — remove the person, and the sentence becomes an instruction.
grammar.mistake: Adding the person back — you cut the vegetables when you mean cut the vegetables. It is not wrong English, but it changes an instruction into a description, and on a packet or a notice it reads oddly. Take the person out.
grammar.tip: Remove the person and the sentence becomes an order.
grammar.practice:
Turn each into an instruction.
1. You boil the water.
2. You cut the vegetables into small pieces.
3. You do not add salt.
4. You heat the pan first.
5. You do not cook it for more than ten minutes.
grammar.answers:
1. Boil the water.  2. Cut the vegetables into small pieces.  3. Do not add salt.  4. Heat the pan first.  5. Do not cook it for more than ten minutes.
Numbers 3 and 5 keep do not at the front — that is how the instruction is made negative. Everything else just loses the word you.

grammar.title: First, then, after that, finally
grammar.explanation: A set of steps without these words is a list. With them it becomes a sequence, and a sequence can be followed by somebody who was not watching you do it.
grammar.rule:
First, heat the oil.
Then cut the vegetables.
After that, add them to the pan.
Next, add a little water.
Finally, take it off the heat.

A comma after the word when it starts the sentence.
(Then usually takes no comma.)

One instruction per step. Not three.
grammar.workedExample:
Put these in order and join them: add the rice · boil the water · cook for ten minutes.
1. What must happen first? The water has to boil before anything goes in it.
2. What next? The rice goes in.
3. What last? It cooks.
4. Now add the ordering words and the commas.
Result:
First, boil the water.
Then add the rice.
After that, cook it for ten minutes.
The order was decided by the cooking, not by the English. Work out the sequence first and then add the words.
grammar.mistake: Putting three instructions into one step — first, heat the oil and cut the vegetables and add the water. It is correct English but it is unusable as an instruction, because the reader cannot tell where one action ends. One step, one thing.
grammar.tip: One step, one instruction. Then a comma after the ordering word.
grammar.practice:
Put these five steps in order and write them out with ordering words and commas.
· add the vegetables
· heat the oil
· take it off the heat
· cut the vegetables
· boil for ten minutes
grammar.answers:
First, heat the oil.
Then cut the vegetables.
After that, add the vegetables.
Next, boil for ten minutes.
Finally, take it off the heat.
Cutting could also come before heating — both work, and either order is correct as long as the vegetables are cut before they go in. What cannot move is the last step.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Ask for ten amounts
speaking.instructions:
Ask for each of these out loud, as you would in a shop.
1 packet of rice · 2 bottles of milk · 3 slices of bread · 1 tin of fish · half a kilo of meat · a bunch of bananas · 2 packets of tea · a piece of cheese · 4 bottles of water · a spoon of sugar
Record all ten. Play it back and check one thing only: did you say of every single time?
speaking.tutor: Order six things from the tutor with amounts, and ask it whether any of the of words were missing.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — At the stall
speaking.instructions:
Say both sides, then change it four times with different items and amounts.
A: Two kilos of rice, please.
B: Anything else?
A: Have you got any fresh fish?
B: Not today.
A: All right. How much is that?
B: Six twenty.
A: Sorry — six twenty?
B: Yes.
Record one full version. Check two things: did you use any in the question, and did you repeat the price back?
speaking.tutor: Buy five things from the tutor, asking the price of each and repeating it back.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Some or any
speaking.instructions:
Say twelve sentences about what is in your kitchen right now.
Four positive, with some. Four negative, with any. Two questions with any. Two requests or offers, with some.
Record all twelve. Play it back and check each one against the type of sentence it was — that is the only thing being tested.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor whether it has any of six things, then offer it some of two things.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Explain how to make something
speaking.instructions:
Choose something simple you can actually cook.
Explain how to make it out loud, in six steps.
Every step must be one instruction, and every step must start with an ordering word.
Record it.
Now the test: play it back and try to follow your own instructions exactly as spoken, doing nothing that was not said. Where would you get stuck? That gap is a missing step.
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor your six steps and ask it to repeat them back in order.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Read the preparation instructions
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3 and read the PREPARATION section out loud.
Then say in your own words what the four instructions are, without looking.
Notice that two of the four are negative — do not boil, do not reheat. Negative instructions are easy to skip when reading quickly and they are usually the important ones.
Record the second part.
speaking.tutor: Read the preparation instructions to the tutor and ask it which ones were negative.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Order a week of food
speaking.instructions:
Without notes, order everything you would need for a week, out loud, in one continuous turn.
At least ten items, each with an amount.
Use at least five different containers or measures.
Ask at least two questions while you do it — about freshness, about price, or about whether they have something.
Record it, listen once, record it again and keep the second.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to be a stallholder and order a week of food from it.

writing.title: Writing 1 — What is in the kitchen
writing.prompt:
Write twelve sentences about the food in your kitchen right now.
Four positive with some, four negative with any, two questions with any, two requests or offers with some.
Underline some or any in each sentence, and write the sentence type in brackets at the end.
writing.model:
1. There is some rice in the cupboard. (positive)
2. I have some milk in the fridge. (positive)
3. There is some bread left. (positive)
4. We have some vegetables. (positive)
5. There is not any fish. (negative)
6. I do not have any meat. (negative)
7. We do not have any tea. (negative)
8. There is not any sugar left. (negative)
9. Is there any milk? (question)
10. Have we got any bread? (question)
11. Would you like some tea? (offer)
12. Can I have some water, please? (request)
writing.criteria: Twelve sentences; four of each of the first two types and two of each of the last two; some or any underlined in each; the type written in brackets; every choice matches its type
writing.support: Write the twelve labels first — positive, positive, positive, positive, negative, and so on — down the page. Then fill in a sentence for each. Choosing the word and the sentence type at the same time is what produces mismatches.
writing.extension: Rewrite the four positive sentences as negatives and watch every some become any.

writing.title: Writing 2 — A recipe somebody could follow
writing.prompt:
Write a recipe for something simple you can actually cook.
Two parts, in this order: what you need, then what you do.
The first part must give amounts with containers or measures.
The second part must be six to eight steps, one instruction each, with ordering words and commas.
Then give it to somebody, or leave it a day and read it as a stranger would.
writing.model:
WHAT YOU NEED
1 packet of rice
2 spoons of oil
3 vegetables (onion, carrot, tomato)
a little salt
1 litre of water

WHAT YOU DO
First, heat the oil in a large pan.
Then cut the vegetables into small pieces.
After that, add the vegetables to the pan and mix them.
Next, add the rice and mix again.
Then add the water and boil it.
After that, cook it for fifteen minutes.
Finally, add a little salt and take it off the heat.
writing.length: A list of what you need and six to eight steps
writing.criteria: Two parts in the right order; every item in the first part has an amount with a container or measure; six to eight steps; one instruction per step; ordering words with commas; no step assumes something the reader has not been told
writing.support: Cook it in your head first, slowly, and write down every physical action as it happens. Do not write the English until the actions are listed — the missing steps are always actions you do without thinking.
writing.extension: Add two negative instructions using do not, and put them where a reader would actually need the warning.

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read a real label
writing.prompt:
Take a real food label from your kitchen.
Write down: the weight, the number of portions, the first three ingredients, the date and which kind of date it is, and one storage instruction.
Then answer two questions in writing: how much salt is in one portion rather than per 100 grams, and how long you have to eat it after opening.
writing.model:
Weight: 400 g, 2 portions of 200 g
First three ingredients: water, carrot, potato
Date: 14 May — this is a USE BY date, so it is about safety
Storage: keep refrigerated below 5 degrees
Salt per portion: 1.8 g, which is twice the per 100 g figure because a portion is 200 g
After opening: 2 days
writing.length: Six pieces of information and two answers
writing.criteria: All six pieces found; the date correctly identified as use by or best before; the per-portion figure correctly calculated rather than copied from the per 100 g column; the after-opening rule found
writing.support: Ingredients are always listed heaviest first — that is a rule, not a coincidence, so the first ingredient tells you what the product mostly is. If the first ingredient is water, it is mostly water.
writing.extension: Compare two labels for similar products and write one sentence about which is saltier per portion.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the eight mistakes
writing.prompt:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. Two packet of rice, please.
2. A bottle milk, please.
3. I do not have some bread.
4. Can I have any water, please?
5. You cut the vegetables, then you add them.  (this is a recipe)
6. Two bottles of waters, please.
7. First heat the oil then cut the vegetables after that add them.
8. Is there some milk?
writing.model:
1. Two packets of rice, please. (Pattern 1 — the s goes on the container)
2. A bottle of milk, please. (Pattern 1 — of is missing)
3. I do not have any bread. (Pattern 2 — negative takes any)
4. Can I have some water, please? (Pattern 2 — a request takes some)
5. Cut the vegetables, then add them. (Pattern 3 — take the person out)
6. Two bottles of water, please. (Pattern 1 — the s goes on the container, not the liquid)
7. First, heat the oil. Then cut the vegetables. After that, add them. (Pattern 4 — one instruction per step, with commas)
8. Is there any milk? (Pattern 2 — a real question takes any)
writing.criteria: All eight corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; no new mistakes introduced
writing.support: Sort them into four piles by pattern before correcting. Three are about containers, three about some and any, one about instructions and one about ordering.
writing.extension: Look back at Writing 2 and check every amount for a missing of.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Which container?
activities.instructions:
Part A. Match the thing to its usual container.
rice · milk · fish · bread · bananas · sugar
packet · bottle · tin · slice · bunch · spoon
Part B. Write the phrase in full.
1. two ____ ____ milk
2. three ____ ____ bread
3. a ____ ____ fish
4. one ____ ____ rice
activities.answers:
Part A. rice–packet, milk–bottle, fish–tin, bread–slice, bananas–bunch, sugar–spoon.
Part B. 1. two bottles of milk  2. three slices of bread  3. a tin of fish  4. one packet of rice.
In Part B every answer needed two words: the container and of. If you wrote two bottles milk, the missing of is the one mistake this pattern has. And the s went on the container every time, never on the thing inside.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Some or any
activities.instructions:
Write some or any, and write the sentence type in brackets.
1. There is ____ rice in the cupboard.
2. We do not have ____ milk.
3. Is there ____ bread left?
4. Would you like ____ tea?
5. Can I have ____ water, please?
6. I did not buy ____ vegetables.
7. Have you got ____ smaller ones?
8. There is ____ fish in the fridge.
9. She does not want ____ sugar.
10. Would you like ____ more?
11. Are there ____ tins left?
12. I bought ____ bread this morning.
activities.answers:
1. some (positive)  2. any (negative)  3. any (question)  4. some (offer)  5. some (request)  6. any (negative)  7. any (question)  8. some (positive)  9. any (negative)  10. some (offer)  11. any (question)  12. some (positive)
Numbers 4, 5 and 10 are the exception — all three are questions in form, but they are offers or requests, so they take some. Numbers 3, 7 and 11 are genuine questions about whether something exists, so they take any.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Put the steps in order
activities.instructions:
These seven steps are in the wrong order. Put them right and write them out with ordering words and commas.
· add the rice and mix it
· take it off the heat
· cut the vegetables
· heat the oil in a large pan
· cook for fifteen minutes
· add the water and boil it
· add the vegetables to the pan
activities.answers:
First, heat the oil in a large pan.
Then cut the vegetables.
After that, add the vegetables to the pan.
Next, add the rice and mix it.
Then add the water and boil it.
After that, cook for fifteen minutes.
Finally, take it off the heat.
Cutting the vegetables could also come first, before the oil is heated — both work. What cannot move is heating before adding, and taking it off the heat last. When you check your answer, ask whether each step is possible at that point, not whether it matches mine exactly.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Statements into instructions
activities.instructions:
Rewrite each as an instruction.
1. You boil the water.
2. You cut the vegetables into small pieces.
3. You do not add salt.
4. You heat the pan first.
5. You put it in the oven for an hour.
6. You do not cook it for more than ten minutes.
7. You mix it well.
8. You do not freeze it.
activities.answers:
1. Boil the water.  2. Cut the vegetables into small pieces.  3. Do not add salt.  4. Heat the pan first.  5. Put it in the oven for an hour.  6. Do not cook it for more than ten minutes.  7. Mix it well.  8. Do not freeze it.
Four of the eight are negative, and all four keep do not at the front. That proportion is deliberate — negative instructions are the ones people skip when reading quickly, and on a label they are usually the important ones.

activities.title: Practice 5 — A real label
activities.instructions:
Take a real packet from your kitchen and find each of these on it.
1. The weight.
2. The number of portions.
3. The first ingredient.
4. Whether it says USE BY or BEST BEFORE.
5. The storage instruction.
6. How long after opening you can keep it.
7. Any allergen warning.
8. One negative instruction, if there is one.
activities.answers:
There is no key — it is your packet. But three things are worth knowing when you look.
Ingredients are listed heaviest first, always. If water is first, the product is mostly water.
Use by is safety and best before is quality. Food after best before is usually fine; food after use by may not be. If a packet has only a use by date, treat that date seriously.
And the after-opening rule can be shorter than the printed date. If a packet says use by 14 May and eat within 2 days of opening, and you open it on the 10th, you have until the 12th, not the 14th. The tighter rule wins.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Say it out loud at the market
activities.instructions:
The next time you buy food, do these three things, and write down afterwards what happened.
1. Say the amount out loud with a container, even if pointing would be quicker.
2. Ask one question you did not need to ask.
3. Repeat the price back before you pay.
Write one line for each: what you said, and what happened.
activities.answers:
No key — the point is what happens.
What most people find: all three worked, none of them caused a problem, and the second one was the hardest to make yourself do. Asking a question you do not need feels like wasting somebody's time, and it is not — it is thirty seconds and it is the only part of the exchange where you learn anything.
If you did the first and third but not the second, do it again this week and only do the second.

quizzes.why: The s goes on the container and of joins it to the thing. Rice itself never takes a plural.
Milk is a liquid, so it comes in a bottle. A packet holds dry things, a slice is cut from something solid, and a bunch is things fastened together.

quizzes.q: Complete: I do not have ____ bread.
quizzes.why: A negative sentence takes any. Some would be right in the positive: I have some bread.

quizzes.q: Complete: Can I have ____ water, please?
quizzes.why: This is a request, not a real question about whether water exists, so it takes some. Can I have any water sounds as though you doubt there is any.
This is a genuine question about whether milk exists, so it takes any. Compare Would you like some milk, which is an offer.

quizzes.q: Which is written as an instruction?
quizzes.why: An instruction starts with the verb and names nobody. The others are a description, a passive statement and advice.

quizzes.q: How do you make an instruction negative?
quizzes.why: Do not add salt. Do not reheat. The rest of the instruction stays exactly as it was.
The other three can be reordered in several workable ways, but nothing can happen after the pan comes off the heat.
An ordering word at the start of a step takes a comma after it. It is a small mark and it makes an instruction much easier to read.

quizzes.q: A label says USE BY 14 May. What kind of date is that?
quizzes.why: Use by is about safety and best before is about quality. Food after its best before date is usually fine; after its use by date it may not be.

quizzes.q: A packet is 400 g and holds 2 portions. Salt is 0.9 g per 100 g. How much salt is in one portion?
quizzes.why: A portion is 200 g, which is twice 100 g, so the salt doubles. Reading only the per 100 g column halves the real amount.

quizzes.q: A label says use by 14 May and eat within 2 days of opening. You open it on 10 May. When must you finish it?
quizzes.why: Two rules apply and the tighter one wins. Two days from opening is 12 May, which comes before the printed use by date.

teacherNotes.note: Every pattern card has a worked example and every exercise an answer key. Practice 5 and Practice 6 send the learner to a real packet and a real market, and both have answer notes that explain what they will probably find rather than giving a correct response — which is the only honest way to key a field task.

teacherNotes.type: Countability is applied here, not taught
teacherNotes.note: Unit 4 taught countable and uncountable twice over, through how much/how many and a little/a few. This unit uses that knowledge to build container phrases and does not explain the distinction again. If a learner struggles with Pattern 1, the problem is almost always Unit 4 rather than this card — send them back rather than reteaching here.

Of is the only real error in Pattern 1, and it is inaudible in fast speech, which is why it survives. A packet rice and a packet of rice sound nearly identical when said quickly. Correct it in writing rather than in speech; that is where it is visible and where it matters.

Practice 4 is deliberately half negative, and the food label carries do not boil, do not freeze and do not reheat. Learners reading quickly skip the do not and read the instruction as positive, which on a real packet can matter. Speaking 5 asks them to identify which instructions were negative for this reason.

The use by against best before distinction is the single most useful thing on a food label and is genuinely not obvious. Three comprehension questions turn on it or on the per 100 g against per portion trap, and one requires noticing that two rules apply at once and the tighter one wins. All three are real and all three cost people money or safety.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner, not a marking service, and no task here is scored by it alone. Learners must not be asked to give the tutor personal details. Note also that this unit touches allergens: the label carries a wheat warning and a traces-of-milk note, and no learner should be encouraged to rely on the course or the tutor for allergen information about real food.

selfAssessment.statement: I can ask for a packet, a bottle or a kilo of something in a shop.
I can say I have some rice and I do not have any rice without mixing them up.
I can read instructions on a packet and do what they say.
I can explain how to do something in steps somebody else could follow.
I can read a food label and tell a use by date from a best before date.

assignment.title: A recipe written, and a label read
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, write a recipe for something you can actually cook, with a what-you-need list giving amounts with containers, and six to eight ordered steps. Then give it to somebody, or leave it a day and follow it yourself doing only what is written, and add one sentence about where a step was missing. Second, take a real food label and record yourself reading out the weight, the portions, the first three ingredients, the date and its type, and the storage rule. Keep both together.
assignment.submissionType: A written recipe and an audio recording
